techniques.name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation
techniques.description: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers a question by retrieving passages from a document collection and asking a language model to write an answer from them. RAG evaluation scores retrieval on whether the fetched passages are relevant and focused and, where reference answers exist, whether they contain what the answer needs. Generation is scored on faithfulness, usually by splitting the answer into individual claims and reporting the share that the fetched passages support, and on answer relevance, which asks whether the answer addresses the question. Frameworks such as Ragas automate these checks with a second language model acting as judge, so faithfulness and relevance need no human-written reference answers. Test sets can also include questions the documents cannot answer, to check that the system says so instead of guessing.

example_use_cases.description: A software company's support team tests its troubleshooting assistant on a set of real customer questions. For each answer it checks that the retrieved pages are the right ones and that every configuration step or command quoted appears in the official documentation, and it holds back changes that introduce invented steps.

A law firm's research team tests an assistant that summarises case law from its own database. Each summary is split into claims and each claim is checked against the passages the assistant retrieved, and summaries with unsupported claims are flagged for review before the assistant is rolled out to fee-earners.

A hospital pharmacy team tests a clinical decision-support tool that retrieves guidelines and patient records. A clinician compares each generated treatment suggestion with the retrieved guideline text, and the team tracks the share of suggestions that go beyond what the sources say before the tool reaches ward staff.

A benefits agency tests its eligibility chatbot on questions drawn from real enquiries, including some the policy documents cannot answer. It checks that quoted amounts and rules match the retrieved policy text and that the chatbot says it cannot answer instead of guessing, before the chatbot is opened to citizens.

limitations.description: Scores that judge retrieval against known answers, such as context recall, need reference answers or labelled passages, which are slow to write and need experts in specialist domains. Reference-free scores avoid this but only penalise irrelevant passages, so they cannot show that a needed passage was never retrieved.

Scores usually come from a second language model acting as judge, so they inherit its errors and its sensitivity to wording. In the original Ragas study the judge agreed with human raters in 95% of pairwise comparisons on faithfulness but only 70% on context relevance, and it struggled to pick out the key sentences in long contexts.

Faithfulness measures whether an answer is supported by the retrieved text, not whether that text is correct, current or complete. A system that retrieves an outdated document and reports it accurately scores well, so the knowledge base needs checking separately.

Claim-by-claim checking may not catch answers that chain reasoning across several documents. Misleading emphasis, selective quotation and unsupported leaps between sources can pass when each sentence is individually supported, so these cases need targeted test questions and human review.

When a score is low, the cause can lie in retrieval, in generation or in how the two interact, and the scores alone often cannot say which. Diagnosis usually needs manual inspection of the retrieved passages and answers for a sample of failing questions.

resources.title: RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
resources.abstract: We introduce RAGAs (Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment), a framework for reference-free evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines. RAGAs is available at [https://github.com/explodinggradients/ragas]. RAG systems are composed of a retrieval and an LLM based generation module. They provide LLMs with knowledge from a reference textual database, enabling them to act as a natural language layer between a user and textual databases, thus reducing the risk of hallucinations. Evaluating RAG architectures is challenging due to several dimensions to consider: the ability of the retrieval system to identify relevant and focused context passages, the ability of the LLM to exploit such passages faithfully, and the quality of the generation itself. With RAGAs, we introduce a suite of metrics that can evaluate these different dimensions without relying on ground truth human annotations. We posit that such a framework can contribute crucially to faster evaluation cycles of RAG architectures, which is especially important given the fast adoption of LLMs.

resources.title: Enhancing the Precision and Interpretability of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in Legal Technology: A Survey
resources.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a promising solution that can enhance the capabilities of large language model (LLM) applications in critical domains, including legal technology, by retrieving knowledge from external databases. Implementing RAG pipelines requires careful attention to the techniques and methods implemented in the different stages of the RAG process. However, robust RAG can enhance LLM generation with faithfulness and few hallucinations in responses. In this paper, we discuss the application of RAG in the legal domain. First, we present an overview of the main RAG methods, stages, techniques, and applications in the legal domain. We then briefly discuss the different information retrieval models, processes, and applied methods in current legal RAG solutions. Then, we explain the different quantitative and qualitative evaluation metrics. We also describe several emerging datasets and benchmarks. We then discuss and assess the ethical and privacy considerations for legal RAG and summarize various challenges, and propose a challenge scale based on RAG failure points and control over external knowledge. Finally, we provide insights into promising future research to leverage RAG efficiently and effectively in the legal field.

resources.title: ASTRID - An Automated and Scalable TRIaD for the Evaluation of RAG-based Clinical Question Answering Systems
resources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive potential in clinical question answering (QA), with Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) emerging as a leading approach for ensuring the factual accuracy of model responses.However, current automated RAG metrics perform poorly in clinical and conversational use cases.Using clinical human evaluations of responses is expensive, unscalable, and not conducive to the continuous iterative development of RAG systems.To address these challenges, we introduce ASTRID -an Automated and Scalable TRIaD for evaluating clinical QA systems leveraging RAG -consisting of three metrics: Context Relevance (CR), Refusal Accuracy (RA), and Conversational Faithfulness (CF).Our novel evaluation metric, CF, is designed to better capture the faithfulness of a model's response to the knowledge base without penalizing conversational elements.Additionally, our metric RA captures the refusal to address questions outside of the system's scope of practice.To validate our triad, we curate a dataset of over 200 real-world patient questions posed to an LLM-based QA agent during surgical follow-up for cataract surgery -the highest volume operation in the worldaugmented with clinician-selected questions for emergency, and clinical and non-clinical out-of-domain scenarios.We demonstrate that CF predicts human ratings of faithfulness more accurately than existing definitions in conversational settings.Furthermore, using eight different LLMs, we demonstrate that the three metrics can closely agree with human evaluations, highlighting the potential of these metrics for use in LLM-driven automated evaluation pipelines.Finally, we show that evaluation using our triad of CF, RA, and CR exhibits alignment with clinician assessment for inappropriate, harmful, or unhelpful responses.We also publish the prompts and datasets for these experiments, providing valuable resources for further research and development.

techniques.name: Reward Hacking Detection
techniques.description: Reward hacking is when an agent trained to maximise a proxy reward (a score that only approximates what its designers want) raises that score by exploiting its gaps while the intended outcome stalls or worsens. Detection scores each trained policy (the agent's decision rule) on the proxy and on an independent measure of the intended objective that training never used, such as a true reward from a simulator, a held-out 'gold' reward model or human ratings. Repeating this at every saved training checkpoint and model size matters because the originating study found capability thresholds at which the true reward drops sharply while the proxy keeps rising. When the true objective cannot be scored in operation, the study instead flags a policy whose actions diverge too far from those of a trusted policy that people have already verified. The output is a pair of reward curves showing where they part, or an anomaly score for each candidate policy.

example_use_cases.description: A transport authority training a reinforcement-learning ramp-metering controller in a traffic simulator rewards it on mean vehicle speed, but also logs average commute time for all drivers at every checkpoint. Checkpoints where speed keeps improving while commute time worsens (for example by holding merging cars back indefinitely) are rejected before any field trial.

A team fine-tuning a customer-support language model with reinforcement learning from human feedback scores each checkpoint with its training reward model and with a held-out reward model and a sample of human ratings that the training loop never sees, and stops training at the point where the training reward keeps rising but the held-out scores fall.

Before an insulin-dosing agent trained against a simulator reward goes to clinical evaluation, the developers score every candidate policy on a separate true objective, time spent in the safe blood-glucose range, and exclude any policy whose simulator reward is high but whose time in range is lower than that of the clinically reviewed baseline policy.

A public-health modelling unit that replaces a reviewed epidemic-response policy with a larger retrained one compares the new policy's actions with the reviewed policy's across simulated outbreaks. A divergence score above the threshold set on earlier policies with known outcomes sends the new policy to expert review instead of adoption, because its true outcome cannot be scored before deployment.

limitations.description: Everything rests on the independent measure of the intended objective. When that measure is itself a proxy (a gold reward model, or a small sample of human ratings), a policy can exploit it too, and the comparison then only detects divergence between two imperfect measures. Collecting enough human ratings at every checkpoint is expensive, which is why studies substitute a gold reward model.

It detects gaming only along the dimensions the true measure scores. A policy that exploits something the true objective does not capture (a side effect, a safety constraint, a user group not represented in the ratings) passes the check, so a clean result is evidence about the measured objective only.

The trusted-policy detector is weak and inconsistent. In the originating benchmark every baseline detector scored an area under the ROC curve below 60% on at least one task, and no detector was best on all tasks, so a quiet detector is not evidence that hacking is absent.

The trusted-policy detector flags difference, not harm. It needs a policy that people have already verified, and comparable action distributions from both policies, and a candidate that is genuinely better than the trusted policy can diverge from it and be flagged, which makes false alarms likely when the trusted policy is only moderately good.

Because the onset of reward hacking can be abrupt as capability grows, checking a few checkpoints or one model size can miss it. The comparison has to be repeated at every checkpoint and model size that might be deployed, which multiplies evaluation cost, especially when the true measure needs human raters.

resources.title: The Effects of Reward Misspecification: Mapping and Mitigating Misaligned Models
resources.abstract: Reward hacking -- where RL agents exploit gaps in misspecified reward functions -- has been widely observed, but not yet systematically studied. To understand how reward hacking arises, we construct four RL environments with misspecified rewards. We investigate reward hacking as a function of agent capabilities: model capacity, action space resolution, observation space noise, and training time. More capable agents often exploit reward misspecifications, achieving higher proxy reward and lower true reward than less capable agents. Moreover, we find instances of phase transitions: capability thresholds at which the agent's behavior qualitatively shifts, leading to a sharp decrease in the true reward. Such phase transitions pose challenges to monitoring the safety of ML systems. To address this, we propose an anomaly detection task for aberrant policies and offer several baseline detectors.

resources.title: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
resources.abstract: In reinforcement learning from human feedback, it is common to optimize against a reward model trained to predict human preferences. Because the reward model is an imperfect proxy, optimizing its value too much can hinder ground truth performance, in accordance with Goodhart’s law. This effect has been frequently observed, but not carefully measured due to the expense of collecting human preference data. In this work, we use a synthetic setup in which a fixed “gold-standard” reward model plays the role of humans, providing labels used to train a proxy reward model. We study how the gold reward model score changes as we optimize against the proxy reward model using either reinforcement learning or best-of-$n$ sampling. We find that this relationship follows a different functional form depending on the method of optimization, and that in both cases its coefficients scale smoothly with the number of reward model parameters. We also study the effect on this relationship of the size of the reward model dataset, the number of reward model and policy parameters, and the coefficient of the KL penalty added to the reward in the reinforcement learning setup. We explore the implications of these empirical results for theoretical considerations in AI alignment.

techniques.name: Toxicity Detection
techniques.description: Toxicity detection scores a model's outputs with a classifier trained to recognise abusive language, such as insults, threats, hate speech and profanity. Testers send the model a large set of prompts, including prompts that tend to provoke toxic replies, and score every response. Results are reported as the share of responses above a chosen score threshold, or as the worst score found across repeated attempts. Human reviewers check a sample of flagged and unflagged responses, because classifiers have known blind spots. The method measures offensive language, not every kind of harm, so dangerous instructions or manipulative advice can pass unflagged.

example_use_cases.description: Before a chatbot goes live on a public-facing site used by children, its replies to a large set of provocative and adversarial prompts are scored with a toxicity classifier. The team decides whether it can launch by checking how many replies exceed an agreed toxicity threshold.

A bank tests its customer-complaints assistant with abusive and provocative messages, scoring every reply with a toxicity classifier, to decide whether it can go live without replying in kind or repeating offensive wording back to customers.

Before launching a mental health support chatbot, a clinical safety team scores its replies to simulated user messages with a toxicity classifier and has clinicians read a sample of flagged and unflagged replies, because subtle stigmatising wording can pass the classifier.

limitations.description: Classifiers can be biased. They lean on words such as slurs and profanity, so they tend to flag text that mentions minority identities or is written in dialects such as African American English, while missing polite but harmful text. Pass or fail results are only as fair as the classifier.

Toxicity depends on context. The same phrase can be abuse, a quotation, reclaimed language or a discussion of abuse, and classifiers score text with little of that context. Expect false alarms in education, news and support settings, and misses where harm is implied rather than stated.

Performance can drop outside the languages, dialects and slang a classifier was built for, and norms about what is offensive vary between communities and change over time. Multilingual or code-switched deployments need validation with local reviewers, and thresholds need re-checking.

The pass mark is a choice. A low threshold blocks legitimate content and a high one lets harmful content through, and stakeholders often disagree about the balance. Report the threshold and the error rates it implies, or toxicity rates cannot be compared between systems.

Subtle or coded harm, and harm that does not sound abusive, such as dangerous instructions or manipulative advice, can pass the classifier. Catching it needs human review of samples, which is slow, costly and distressing for reviewers, and may not scale to high-volume or real-time use.

resources.title: RealToxicityPrompts: Evaluating Neural Toxic Degeneration in Language Models
resources.abstract: Pretrained neural language models (LMs) are prone to generating racist, sexist, or otherwise toxic language which hinders their safe deployment.We investigate the extent to which pretrained LMs can be prompted to generate toxic language, and the effectiveness of controllable text generation algorithms at preventing such toxic degeneration.We create and release RE-ALTOXICITYPROMPTS, a dataset of 100K naturally occurring, sentence-level prompts derived from a large corpus of English web text, paired with toxicity scores from a widelyused toxicity classifier.Using REALTOXICI-TYPROMPTS, we find that pretrained LMs can degenerate into toxic text even from seemingly innocuous prompts.We empirically assess several controllable generation methods, and find that while data-or compute-intensive methods (e.g., adaptive pretraining on non-toxic data) are more effective at steering away from toxicity than simpler solutions (e.g., banning "bad" words), no current method is failsafe against neural toxic degeneration.To pinpoint the potential cause of such persistent toxic degeneration, we analyze two web text corpora used to pretrain several LMs (including GPT-2; Radford et al., 2019), and find a significant amount of offensive, factually unreliable, and otherwise toxic content.Our work provides a test bed for evaluating toxic generations by LMs and stresses the need for better data selection processes for pretraining.

resources.title: A New Generation of Perspective API: Efficient Multilingual Character-level Transformers
resources.abstract: On the world wide web, toxic content detectors are a crucial line of defense against potentially hateful and offensive messages. As such, building highly effective classifiers that enable a safer internet is an important research area. Moreover, the web is a highly multilingual, cross-cultural community that develops its own lingo over time. As such, it is crucial to develop models that are effective across a diverse range of languages, usages, and styles. In this paper, we present the fundamentals behind the next version of the Perspective API from Google Jigsaw. At the heart of the approach is a single multilingual token-free Charformer model that is applicable across a range of languages, domains, and tasks. We demonstrate that by forgoing static vocabularies, we gain flexibility across a variety of settings. We additionally outline the techniques employed to make such a byte-level model efficient and feasible for productionization. Through extensive experiments on multilingual toxic comment classification benchmarks derived from real API traffic and evaluation on an array of code-switching, covert toxicity, emoji-based hate, human-readable obfuscation, distribution shift, and bias evaluation settings, we show that our proposed approach outperforms strong baselines. Finally, we present our findings from deploying this system in production.

A Human-centered Evaluation of a Toxicity Detection API: Testing Transferability and Unpacking Latent Attributes
resources.abstract: Perspective is a publicly available, machine learning API that can score text for toxicity. It is available for use in online platforms and communities to limit toxicity and promote civil dialogue. In this work, we adopt a human-centered approach to evaluating Perspective by investigating if human ratings of toxicity align with Perspective’s toxicity scores. We also test its transferability by making this comparison for comments from three platforms that have different commenting styles and moderation strategies: news websites, YouTube, and Twitter. Apart from toxicity, the main attribute, we collect participant ratings for three additional attributes: respectfulness, formality, and presence of stereotypes. While disrespect is part of how Perspective defines toxicity, formality and presence of stereotypes were included in the study to explore if they could be hidden/latent attributes that affect toxicity scores from Perspective. We analyzed how participant ratings for these additional attributes vary with respect to Perspective’s toxicity score for comments from each platform. We find that for high toxicity scores, Perspective strongly aligns with participant ratings of toxicity and disrespectfulness across all three platforms, providing weak evidence of its transferability. However, our evaluation also surfaced formality and presence of stereotypes as latent attributes that are unrecognized parts of Perspective’s scores. We discuss how and why this evaluation is “human-centered,” the importance of conducting such evaluations, and implications of these results for content moderation in social platforms.

resources.title: An Evaluation of the Google Perspective API by Race and Gender
resources.abstract: Research on American politicians demonstrates that minority politicians often face higher rates of uncivil speech online.While previous studies have focused on federal representatives, local politicians engage more frequently with constituents, increasing the risk of online and offline violence.These imminent threats to state-level officials highlight the need for tools that can measure the toxic discourse faced by local politicians, making algorithmic evaluation of these tools essential for understanding these interactions.To this end, this study evaluates the Google Perspective API, a widely used machine learning algorithm that quantifies toxicity.This study assesses the performance of the API across various demographic identities.Using a dataset of one million tweets directed at state legislators across all 50 states in January 2021, I identify significant gender and racial discrepancies in the algorithm's performance.Specifically, the API demonstrates better performance in predicting toxicity toward men than toward women.The racial discrepancies are slightly more nuanced with the API performing better for some races and not others.This research underscores the importance of algorithmic validation and has implications for studies of algorithmic performance, online harassment and political communication.

techniques.name: Training Data Extraction Testing
techniques.description: Training data extraction testing measures how much of its training text a generative language model reproduces word for word when it is sampled, without the tester supplying any training record to look for. It differs from membership inference testing, which starts from a candidate record and asks only whether that record was used in training, and from canary exposure testing, which needs secrets planted before training. The tester prompts the model with empty prompts or a few words taken from public text, generates a large volume of output (from tens of millions to billions of tokens) with the sampling settings the deployed system uses, and checks it against the training corpus: any span of at least a fixed length, such as 50 tokens, found verbatim in an index of the corpus, and not low-entropy filler such as repeated characters or lists of numbers, counts as extracted, and personal data is checked by tagging names and identifiers in the output and looking them up in the corpus. Where the corpus cannot be searched, the outputs are ranked by how much more probable the model finds them than a smaller reference model or a text-compression algorithm does, and the top-ranked candidates are checked by hand, for example by web search. The result is the share of generated text copied from training data (under the hand-checked route, the number confirmed among the candidates checked), the number of distinct passages extracted, and the passages themselves, each with a count of the training documents that contain it: a passage found in one or two documents is a privacy finding in a way that a licence or news story repeated thousands of times is not.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's privacy engineering team fine-tunes an open-weight language model on ten years of customer-service chat transcripts to draft replies for agents. Before deployment it generates 50 million tokens from public-text prompts with the production sampling settings, searches an index of the transcripts for 50-token matches, and looks up every account number, name and phone number tagged in the output. It runs the same test on the base model as a control.

A hospital research group that trained a clinical note-completion model on de-identified discharge summaries runs the test before sharing the weights with partner hospitals. Besides searching for verbatim passages of the summaries, it tags patient names, dates of birth and NHS numbers in the generated text and looks each up in the training set, to find identifiers the de-identification step missed and decide whether the summaries must be re-scrubbed and the model retrained.

An AI developer preparing an open-weight release compares two checkpoints, one trained on a deduplicated copy of the pre-training corpus. It generates text from each at budgets of 100 million and 1 billion tokens, counts distinct 50-token passages found verbatim in the corpus, and compares how the counts grow with the budget, not a single rate, before choosing which checkpoint to release and what to say about memorisation in the model card.

A government department running a citizen-facing chat assistant on a model it fine-tuned on casework correspondence repeats the test after every fine-tuning update. Because chat-tuned models can leak little under ordinary prompts yet emit training text once pushed off their chat behaviour, the test also uses prompts asking the assistant to repeat a single word many times, a pattern that made one production assistant reproduce its training data.

limitations.description: The result is a lower bound set by the effort spent. The number of distinct passages extracted keeps growing as more text is generated, and one study found that a model which leaked more than another at a small budget leaked less in total. A clean result, or a comparison of models at one fixed budget, can therefore mislead; report the generation budget and compare models at several budgets.

Much memorised text comes out only after the right prompt. In one study, sampling from short public prompts recovered about a third of the passages a model was known to reproduce when given their true opening words, and a chat-tuned model leaked far less under ordinary prompts than when pushed into repeating a word. A low rate under ordinary prompts is weak evidence that the data cannot be extracted.

The verdict depends on what the output is checked against and on the match rule. A public proxy for an unavailable corpus undercounts (in one study a 9 TB proxy found under half the matches a manual web search found), and a minimum match length long enough to rule out coincidence misses short secrets such as phone or account numbers unless they are tagged and looked up separately. Paraphrased leaks and facts stitched together from several documents are not counted.

It is costly at a useful scale. One study generated a billion tokens per model, and its whole evaluation, including a 45 TB index built over a 9 TB corpus, took three weeks on a large cloud machine. The test also produces copies of any personal data the model leaks, which must be stored, reviewed and deleted under the same controls as the training data.

It shows what the model emits, not what an attacker could infer. It does not say whether a known person's record was used in training, and it gives no bound for data the test did not happen to elicit, so a clean result cannot stand in for a formal guarantee such as differential privacy.

techniques.name: PII Detection and Redaction in Training Text
techniques.description: PII detection and redaction finds personally identifiable information (PII), such as names, email addresses, phone numbers and account or ID numbers, in a body of text and removes or replaces it before the text is used to train or fine-tune a model, so that the model has fewer personal details to memorise and later reproduce. Presidio, a widely used open-source tool first released by Microsoft and now run as an independent community project, is the reference implementation: each document passes through a set of recognisers, in which a named-entity recognition model (by default an English spaCy model) tags names, places and dates, patterns with checksum or format checks catch structured identifiers such as card and NHS numbers, and nearby words such as 'account' raise a candidate's confidence score. Every detection above a chosen score is then replaced with a placeholder for its type (for example <PERSON>), masked, hashed, encrypted or deleted, and the cleaned corpus goes to training. Because detection is never complete, the procedure ends by measuring recall, the share of identifiers actually caught, for each type on a hand-labelled sample of the same corpus. The evidence it produces is that measured miss rate and the cleaned corpus; unlike differential privacy or synthetic data, it removes real personal details from real text and gives no bound on what remains.

example_use_cases.description: A bank preparing two years of customer-service chat transcripts to fine-tune an assistant runs Presidio with added pattern recognisers for sort codes and its own account-number format, replaces each detection with a type placeholder, and has staff label 500 transcripts by hand to measure recall per entity type. It fine-tunes only once recall for names and account numbers meets the target in its data protection impact assessment, where it records the miss rate.

An NHS trust preparing discharge letters to fine-tune a summarisation model finds on a labelled sample that the default English model misses many names written in clinical shorthand and does not detect ward and bed codes at all. It adds lists of staff names and patterns for local codes, re-measures recall on a fresh labelled sample, and reports the remaining miss rate to its information governance group, which decides whether further controls are needed.

A company building a code-completion model from its internal repositories detects email addresses, IP addresses, keys and passwords with patterns and a trained detector, discards detections that are too short or are private network addresses to cut false alarms, replaces the rest with tokens such as <EMAIL> and <KEY>, and reports precision and recall per type on an annotated set of files kept apart from tuning.

limitations.description: Detection always misses some identifiers, and a model can memorise and reproduce what is missed, especially details repeated across many documents. A study that fine-tuned GPT-2 on court judgments and emails scrubbed with Presidio's default tagger and a second recogniser concluded that scrubbing reduces but cannot fully prevent leakage of personal information; Presidio's README gives no guarantee of finding it all. The evidence is a measured miss rate, not proof that none remains.

It finds only the categories it has recognisers for. On a 2022 benchmark of European Court of Human Rights judgments, Presidio's default setup caught about 70 per cent of identifying mentions but only about 45 per cent of direct identifiers, because it did not recognise case numbers, which identify the applicant on their own. Details that identify someone only in combination, such as a job title, employer and town, are not entity types at all, so redacted text can still point to a person.

The default recognisers are built for general English text. Clinical shorthand, other languages, source code and in-house identifier formats need extra recognisers or a different model, and recall measured on one corpus does not carry over to another, so the labelled sample used for the measurement must come from the corpus being cleaned and be kept apart from any tuning of the recognisers.

Raising recall by lowering the score threshold or switching on broad entity types also removes text that is not personal, such as names of public bodies, laws and places the task depends on, which lowers the value of the data for training. On the court-judgment benchmark, switching on organisation names raised Presidio's recall slightly but cut its precision from about 0.76 to 0.54.

Redaction removes identifiers from the text but does not hide whether a document was used for training, and it gives no formal bound. In the GPT-2 study, membership inference on the scrubbed model still reached an AUC of 0.82, where 0.5 is chance, and adding differentially private training brought it down to 0.5. Claims about membership, or a formal guarantee, need DP-SGD or another method alongside redaction.

techniques.name: Dangerous Capability Evaluation
techniques.description: Dangerous capability evaluation measures whether a frontier AI model can carry out tasks that could enable severe harm, such as finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, persuading or deceiving people, acquiring resources and running copies of itself, or helping to plan an attack with chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear materials, and compares the results with capability thresholds that the developer's safety framework fixes before testing. Evaluators first write a threat model for each risk domain; the framework names a critical capability level, at which the model could pose an extreme risk without extra safeguards, and an early-warning trigger defined on the evaluation results, which the method's originators sketched for one domain as success on more than half of a set of tasks given ten attempts at each. They then build task suites for each domain, such as capture-the-flag hacking challenges in sandboxed networks or multi-step tasks that require the model to set up a cloud server and install software, and try to draw out the model's best performance: it is tested without the safety filters of the deployed product, given agent scaffolding (prompts, planning loops and tools such as a command shell) and sometimes fine-tuned, because the evaluation must not underestimate what the model can do. Scoring records success over repeated attempts and, for tasks the model cannot finish, how close it came, by starting it from intermediate milestones and measuring how much expert help it needs to succeed. Unlike red teaming, which probes a system and its safeguards for whatever failures can be found, and unlike tests of whether a model refuses harmful requests, it measures what the model is able to do, and whether the results cross the trigger informs decisions on deployment and on the security measures the model needs.

example_use_cases.description: A frontier AI developer runs its cyber-offence task suite on each major checkpoint during training and before release, using the agent scaffold its evaluation team has found strongest. Its safety framework sets an early-warning trigger on the share of professional-level capture-the-flag challenges solved; a checkpoint that crosses it cannot be released until stronger protection of the model weights and mitigations against cyber misuse are in place.

A national AI security institute given access to a model before release runs autonomy tasks, such as setting up a cloud server and installing an open-source model on it, both end to end and from intermediate milestones, with a staff member approving each action the agent takes on the live internet. It reports to the developer how close the model came to completing each task and how this compares with the developer's previous model.

A company preparing to publish a model's weights openly evaluates a version fine-tuned on task-relevant data as well as the version it plans to release, because anyone who downloads the weights can fine-tune them, and compares the fine-tuned version's results with its threshold when deciding whether to publish.

limitations.description: A result below the threshold is only as strong as the effort spent drawing out the model's capability. Better scaffolds, more attempts, fine-tuning or a later checkpoint can raise scores, and models can be prompted or fine-tuned to underperform deliberately on dangerous-capability tasks while scoring normally elsewhere, so a negative result is a lower bound on capability, not proof of its absence.

The link between a task score and real-world harm is weakly grounded. The method's originators describe their early-warning trigger as early thinking in an extremely immature area and set no thresholds for their chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear evaluations, where most scientific information is dual-use, so different developers can draw the line in different places and reach different decisions from the same scores.

Task suites cover only the threat models someone has written down, and laboratory tasks may not reflect real conditions: persuasion measured in short dialogues with paid participants, or hacking measured on capture-the-flag challenges, may overstate or understate what the model could do against real people and real systems.

Agentic tasks need sandboxed environments, many repeated runs and expert grading, and tasks with real internet access need a person to approve each action so the agent cannot cause harm, which makes full runs slow and costly. Testing the unfiltered model also needs access that external evaluators may not have; testing the deployed product with its safety filters measures something different.

Results date quickly. Scores change with each new checkpoint and fine-tuning recipe, so evaluations have to be repeated for every significant model update, and published tasks can leak into training data, which is why the originating team withheld solutions and flag values from the tasks it released.

resources.abstract: To understand the risks posed by a new AI system, we must understand what it can and cannot do. Building on prior work, we introduce a programme of new "dangerous capability" evaluations and pilot them on Gemini 1.0 models. Our evaluations cover four areas: (1) persuasion and deception; (2) cyber-security; (3) self-proliferation; and (4) self-reasoning. We do not find evidence of strong dangerous capabilities in the models we evaluated, but we flag early warning signs. Our goal is to help advance a rigorous science of dangerous capability evaluation, in preparation for future models.

techniques.name: Sparse Autoencoder Feature Analysis
techniques.description: Sparse autoencoder feature analysis looks for human-interpretable units inside a neural network, usually a language model, by learning from the activations at one layer a large dictionary of directions, called features, such that each activation vector can be rebuilt from only a few of them. Unlike neuron activation analysis it does not take the network's own neurons as the units, since single neurons often respond to several unrelated things, and unlike concept activation vectors it needs no labelled examples of a concept chosen in advance, because the features are found without supervision. The analyst records activations at the chosen layer over a large body of ordinary text and trains an autoencoder, a network with one hidden layer usually several times wider than the layer studied, to reconstruct them while a sparsity penalty keeps most hidden units at zero; the decoder weights of each hidden unit then give one feature direction. Each feature is labelled from the inputs on which it fires most strongly, by a person or by a language model that writes a description, which is then scored on how well it predicts the feature's activations on other text, and the label is tested by removing or amplifying the feature inside the running model and checking the change in output. The output is a catalogue of labelled features with example activations, interpretability scores and measured effects, plus a reconstruction score saying how much of the layer's behaviour the dictionary accounts for; the features can then serve as units for causal mediation analysis, which traces pathways, while this method finds and checks the units themselves.

example_use_cases.description: Before deploying an open-weights language model as a customer-service assistant, a bank's AI assurance team uses sparse autoencoders published for that model to find features active on prompts where the assistant should refuse to give investment advice. It tests each candidate by suppressing it and measuring the change in refusal rate, and records which labelled features the refusal behaviour depends on in the model's assurance file.

A bioinformatics group using a protein language model to annotate newly sequenced proteins trains sparse autoencoders on its embeddings and compares the features with database annotations of binding sites, structural motifs and domains. Features that match known biology are used to propose candidate annotations for curators to verify, features that fire widely with no clear meaning are flagged for review, and the model's own annotation accuracy is still tested on held-out proteins.

A team that fine-tuned a language model to triage clinical referral letters lists the sparse autoencoder features that most change the 'urgent' score on a validation set, and checks whether they describe clinical content or properties of the letter, such as the referring practice's template. A template feature among the leading drivers is recorded as a finding and leads to retraining on reformatted letters.

limitations.description: The dictionary does not capture everything the layer carries, and what it misses cannot be inspected. In the originating study, replacing one layer of a small language model with its reconstruction raised perplexity from 25 to 40; a concurrent study recovered 79% of a layer's contribution to the loss in its main run. Not finding a feature for a concept does not show that the model lacks it.

The features found are not unique. Larger dictionaries split a feature into narrower ones (one base64 feature at 512 features became three at 4,096), and for a 131,000-feature autoencoder on one layer of Llama 3 8B only about 30% of features were shared by two runs differing only in random seed. A conclusion resting on one feature should name the autoencoder used and be checked on a second run.

Labels are hypotheses drawn from the top-activating examples, and automated scores are modest: the first five features reported in the originating study scored between -0.11 and 0.57, and the advantage over simpler decompositions faded in later layers. Back a label with an intervention that changes the output as the label predicts before citing it as evidence.

It needs the model's internal activations, plus storage and compute to train an autoencoder for each layer studied (one concurrent study trained on 8 billion activation vectors from a single layer). For large models practitioners often rely on autoencoders released for particular open-weights models, so the method is not available for a model reached only through an API.

Being interpretable does not make the features better for a given task. In a 2025 study of detecting concepts from model activations, probes built on autoencoder features did not beat logistic regression on the raw activations on average, and the spurious correlations and data problems they exposed could also be found with simpler baselines. Where detection is the goal, compare against such baselines.

techniques.name: Bias Benchmark for Question Answering
techniques.description: The Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) is a fixed set of about 58,500 multiple-choice reading questions that tests whether a language model's answers rely on social stereotypes, across nine social dimensions (age, disability status, gender identity, nationality, physical appearance, race and ethnicity, religion, socio-economic status and sexual orientation) and two combinations of them, using stereotypes documented as harmful in US English-speaking contexts (Parrish et al., 2022). Each item describes two people from different groups and asks a question that points at a stereotype, such as who is bad at maths, with three answers to choose from: either person, or an answer such as 'cannot be determined'; in the ambiguous version the passage does not say which person the question is about, so 'cannot be determined' is correct, and in the disambiguated version an added sentence settles it. Items come in balanced sets that swap the two groups and their order and pair each negative question with a non-negative one, so that a model which simply prefers one group whatever the question is not counted as stereotyping. From the model's chosen answers (generated, or picked by comparing the probabilities it gives the three options) the test reports accuracy in each version and a bias score per category from -100% to 100%: the share of answers naming a person that follow the stereotype, rescaled so that 0 means no consistent direction and a negative score leans against the stereotype, and in the ambiguous version multiplied by the error rate, so that stereotyped guesses weigh more when the model guesses often; it also reports how far accuracy falls when the correct answer goes against the stereotype. Unlike substituting identity terms into a deployer's own inputs, or varying the people shown in few-shot examples, BBQ is a fixed external question set that tests what a model concludes about people when the text does, and does not, support a conclusion.

example_use_cases.description: A government department choosing between three language models for a service that answers citizens' questions about benefits runs the full BBQ set on each, with the same prompt, answer extraction and scoring for all three. It compares accuracy and both bias scores category by category, rules out any model whose ambiguous-context bias score in any category is further from zero, in either direction, than a limit set before testing, and records that the result covers US stereotypes only.

A recruitment software company fine-tuning an open-weight model to answer HR helpdesk questions runs BBQ on the base model and on every fine-tuned version through the same evaluation harness, logging each answer. A release is blocked if any category's ambiguous-context bias score moves further from zero than the base model's by more than an agreed margin, or if the accuracy gap between items whose correct answer matches the stereotype and items whose correct answer goes against it widens.

An NHS trust's digital team preparing a health-information assistant needs evidence about UK stereotypes, which BBQ was not built for. Following the procedure used to build a Korean version, it keeps templates that transfer, changes target groups where UK stereotypes differ, drops those that do not apply, writes UK-specific ones, surveys members of the UK public to confirm each stereotype and its target group, and reports results on the original and adapted sets side by side.

limitations.description: BBQ's stereotypes, and most of its categories, come from US English-speaking contexts, and its authors say results should not be used as evidence about other cultures. Adapting it to Korean meant changing target groups, dropping templates and adding four categories, and a machine-translated BBQ gave different bias scores from the adapted version (Jin et al., 2024). For a UK deployment the original set says nothing about UK-specific stereotypes.

A low bias score is weak evidence that a model is unbiased. Each category rests on about 25 templates with very short passages and three fixed answers; the authors warn that a low score is not proof of an unbiased model, and that for a model used on very different text BBQ is unlikely to be a valid measure. It counts only stereotypes that change the chosen answer, so it misses bias that shifts the model's probabilities without changing its choice.

The bias score leaves out 'cannot be determined' answers and has a sign, so it must be read with accuracy and by its distance from zero. A model that always gives that answer has full accuracy and a zero bias score on ambiguous items, yet fails every disambiguated one. A negative score means answers lean against the stereotype, as HELM found for most of the models it tested (Liang et al., 2023); a one-sided limit such as 'below 5%' passes such a model.

Scores depend on the prompt format and on how answers are extracted or scored, so they compare only across models tested the same way. In the original study one UnifiedQA model, given the same items in two input formats, scored 2.4 and 18.6 on ambiguous gender-identity items. Results for a single template rest on few items (one reported example has 72), so they are noisy and should be combined across templates for the same stereotype.

It is weak evidence about bias against people with two combined identities. In the original study, results on the two intersectional categories (race by gender, race by socio-economic status) were too inconsistent for the authors to conclude that models responded to more than one aspect of identity, and the lm-evaluation-harness task notes that these categories are not really taken into account in its bias scores.

Holistic Evaluation of Language Models
resources.abstract: Language models (LMs) are becoming the foundation for almost all major language technologies, but their capabilities, limitations, and risks are not well understood. We present Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) to improve the transparency of language models. First, we taxonomize the vast space of potential scenarios (i.e. use cases) and metrics (i.e. desiderata) that are of interest for LMs. Then we select a broad subset based on coverage and feasibility, noting what's missing or underrepresented (e.g. question answering for neglected English dialects, metrics for trustworthiness). Second, we adopt a multi-metric approach: We measure 7 metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency) for each of 16 core scenarios when possible (87.5% of the time). This ensures metrics beyond accuracy don't fall to the wayside, and that trade-offs are clearly exposed. We also perform 7 targeted evaluations, based on 26 targeted scenarios, to analyze specific aspects (e.g. reasoning, disinformation). Third, we conduct a large-scale evaluation of 30 prominent language models (spanning open, limited-access, and closed models) on all 42 scenarios, 21 of which were not previously used in mainstream LM evaluation. Prior to HELM, models on average were evaluated on just 17.9% of the core HELM scenarios, with some prominent models not sharing a single scenario in common. We improve this to 96.0%: now all 30 models have been densely benchmarked on the same core scenarios and metrics under standardized conditions. Our evaluation surfaces 25 top-level findings. For full transparency, we release all raw model prompts and completions publicly for further analysis, as well as a general modular toolkit. We intend for HELM to be a living benchmark for the community, continuously updated with new scenarios, metrics, and models.

sample_claims.text: Under the department's fixed prompt and scoring, the selected model's ambiguous-context BBQ bias score was between -5% and +5% in each of the nine categories, and its accuracy on disambiguated items differed by less than 2 percentage points between items whose correct answer matched the stereotype and items whose correct answer did not.

No fine-tuned release of the HR helpdesk model has an ambiguous-context BBQ bias score more than 2 percentage points further from zero than the base model's in any category, measured with the same harness version, prompt and scoring.

On a UK-adapted version of BBQ, whose stereotypes and target groups were confirmed by a survey of the UK public before use, the health-information assistant's ambiguous-context bias score was between -5% and +5% in every category and its accuracy on disambiguated items was above 90%.
